content: The EN1 gene encodes the homeobox protein engrailed-1 in humans. Homeobox-containing genes are believed to play a significant role in regulating developmental processes. In Drosophila, the engrailed (en) gene is crucial for proper segmentation during development, as it is necessary for the formation of posterior compartments. Mutations in the mouse homologs of this gene, EN1 and EN2, result in various developmental abnormalities, many of which are lethal. The human homologs of engrailed, EN1 and EN2, encode proteins containing homeodomains and are implicated in the regulation of pattern formation during the development of the central nervous system. The engrailed-1 (EN1) gene is a homeobox gene that primarily regulates development in the dorsal midbrain and anterior hindbrain, which includes the cerebellum and colliculi, in humans. The expression of EN1 is regulated by fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8) until 13 days post-fertilization. FGF8 controls the development of the forebrain and hindbrain. EN1 expression is initially active for approximately 12 hours around day 5 post-fertilization, after which EN2 expression begins. Once EN2 is expressed, EN1 is re-expressed in other tissues, such as somites and limb ectoderm, throughout development. A knockout mouse model was created in which the EN1 homeobox was deleted. These mice died within 24 hours of birth because they refused to feed, despite having the physical ability to do so. Upon examination of the brains of these mice, it was found that most of the cerebellum, colliculi, and cranial nerves III and IV were absent. All of the mice exhibited significant forepaw deformities, including fusion of digits and the presence of a sixth digit. Additionally, the 13th ribs and sternum showed delayed and abnormal ossification. This mouse model demonstrated that EN1 expression is critical for the proper development of the brain, limbs, and sternum.
